@@id.summary: @@id defines a composite primary key using multiple scalar fields on a Prisma model. The combined field values identify each record and can be referenced through Prisma Client.
@@id.explanation: The @@id block defines a model's primary key from multiple scalar fields. Prisma treats the combined values as one identifier and exposes the composite key in Client queries using a generated name based on the participating fields, unless you provide a custom name.
@@id.syntax: @@id(_ fields: FieldReference[], name: String?, map: String?)

parameters.name: fields
parameters.description: The scalar fields that together form the composite primary key.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Optional custom name for the composite ID in Prisma Client.

parameters.name: map
parameters.description: Optional database constraint name mapped by Prisma.

@@id.returns: Defines a composite primary key for the model; Prisma Client exposes the composite identifier for query operations.

example.explanation: This model uses the pair of fields as one composite primary key.

useCases.title: Model compound identity
useCases.scenario: A record is uniquely determined by two or more values, such as a user and a post in a join model.

useCases.title: Reflect an existing relational key
useCases.scenario: A database table already uses a multi-column primary key that the Prisma schema must represent.

useCases.title: Name the Client selector
useCases.scenario: Application code needs a readable composite-key selector instead of Prisma's generated field-name combination.

interview.question: What does @@id do?
interview.answer: @@id defines a multi-field primary key on a model. The combined values identify a record, and the corresponding database type is a PRIMARY KEY.
interview.followUp: How does Prisma Client name an unnamed composite key? By default, it combines the field names with underscores, such as postId_userId.

interview.question: How do you declare a composite ID?
interview.answer: Use the fields argument with an array of scalar field names, for example @@id([postId, userId]). The fields argument itself may be omitted in this shorthand form.
interview.followUp: How can the generated Prisma Client key name be changed? Add a name argument, such as @@id(name: "likeId", fields: [postId, userId]).

interview.question: What database limitation applies to @@id?
interview.answer: A composite ID is supported for relational databases but not by MongoDB. In MongoDB, a model must use one field marked with @id and mapped to _id.
interview.followUp: Can a composite ID be placed on a relation field? No; the participating fields must be scalar fields.

keyPoints: Use @@id to make several model fields jointly serve as the primary key.
The database identifies a record from the combined values of all fields listed in the block.
For relational connectors, @@id maps to the database's PRIMARY KEY concept.
You can write the compact form @@id([fieldA, fieldB]) instead of naming the fields argument.
Without a custom name, Prisma Client derives the composite-key selector name by joining field names with underscores.
gotchas: MongoDB cannot use @@id; its IDs must be represented by a single field with @id and @map("_id").
Fields participating in a composite ID cannot be optional.
Only scalar fields such as String, Int, and enum can participate directly; relation fields cannot.

@@index.syntax: @@index(_ fields: FieldReference[], map: String?, where: raw(String) | { field: value }?)

parameters.name: fields
parameters.description: One or more model field references included in the index; the fields argument name may be omitted.

parameters.name: map
parameters.description: Optional database index name mapping.

parameters.name: where
parameters.description: Optional partial-index predicate, expressed as raw SQL or a type-safe object.

@@index.returns: Declares an index in the database.

example.title: Composite model index
example.explanation: This model declares a database index spanning the title and content fields.

useCases.title: Speed up common lookups
useCases.scenario: Queries frequently filter or sort by a model field.

useCases.title: Create a multi-column index
useCases.scenario: A relational query benefits from a combined lookup across fields.

useCases.title: Configure an advanced index

interview.question: What does @@index do?
interview.answer: @@index declares an index in the database at the model level. Its field list can contain one field or multiple fields, such as @@index([title, content]).
interview.followUp: How would you name the underlying database index? Use the optional map argument to control the database constraint or index name.

interview.question: How is the field list specified?
interview.answer: The positional form @@index([title, author]) is equivalent to @@index(fields: [title, author]); the fields argument name is optional. Field-level length and sort options are written alongside the relevant field.
interview.followUp: How can a MongoDB composite-type field be indexed? Use dot notation such as @@index([address.number]) where supported.

interview.question: Are all @@index options portable across databases?
interview.answer: Index configuration varies by database. For example, PostgreSQL supports access methods such as Hash, Gist, Gin, SpGist, and Brin through the type argument, while MySQL supports length configuration for indexed String and Bytes subparts.
interview.followUp: What should be checked before using an advanced argument? Verify that the target database provider supports that argument on @@index.

keyPoints: @@index adds a database index to the model.
You may write the fields array directly without the fields: label.
A single declaration can cover multiple fields for relational database models.
Per-field length and sort settings are placed inside the indexed field list.
The type argument configures the index access method where the provider supports it.
gotchas: Partial-index predicates use either a raw SQL expression or a type-safe object literal; choose the form supported by the documentation and database.
Composite indexes are documented for relational databases; do not assume the same multi-field behavior applies to every provider.

@@map.summary: `@@map` maps a Prisma model to a differently named database table or MongoDB collection. It lets Prisma Client use a clean model name while preserving the database object's existing name.
@@map.explanation: Add `@@map` to a model to decouple its Prisma name from the underlying database object. Prisma Client uses the model name, while relational databases use the mapped table name and MongoDB uses the mapped collection name.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Database table name for relational databases, or collection name for MongoDB; the page also allows an underlying enum name.

@@map.returns: No runtime value; this schema attribute controls the database object name used by Prisma ORM.

example.title: Map a model to an existing table
example.explanation: This keeps the Prisma model name `Comment` while reading and writing the existing `comments` table.

useCases.title: Preserve database naming
useCases.scenario: A database table is named `comments`, but the schema should use the singular `Comment` model.

useCases.title: Work with legacy schemas
useCases.scenario: An existing database uses names that do not follow Prisma model naming conventions.

useCases.title: Separate API and storage names
useCases.scenario: The Prisma Client API should use domain-friendly model names without changing stored database object names.

interview.question: What does `@@map` do?
interview.answer: `@@map` maps a Prisma model name to a different database table or MongoDB collection name. This lets Prisma Client expose a model such as `Comment` while the database object is named `comments`.
interview.followUp: How would you map a field as well? Use field-level `@map`, for example `text String @map("comment_text")`; `@@map` applies to the model, whereas `@map` applies to a field or enum value.

interview.question: What argument does `@@map` take?
interview.answer: Its required `name` value is the database table name for relational databases or collection name for MongoDB. The attribute can use either `@@map("users")` or `@@map(name: "users")`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the attribute is omitted? Prisma uses the model name itself as the table or collection name.

interview.question: Why use `@@map`?
interview.answer: Use `@@map` when the database uses naming conventions or legacy names that differ from the names preferred in the Prisma schema. Prisma Client then remains idiomatic without requiring the underlying database object to be renamed.
interview.followUp: Can `@@map` rename an enum in the database? Yes; the schema reference also documents mapping an enum name to a different underlying database enum.

keyPoints: `@@map` connects a Prisma model to a differently named relational table or MongoDB collection.
The same attribute can map an enum name to a different database enum.
The required mapped value identifies the database table or collection that Prisma should use.
The `name` label is optional, so named and positional syntax are equivalent.
gotchas: Without `@@map`, Prisma expects the model name to match the relational table or MongoDB collection name.
Both named and positional forms are valid, so `@@map(name: "users")` and `@@map("users")` mean the same thing.

@@unique.explanation: Place @@unique on a model to require that the combination of listed fields is unique. Prisma creates the corresponding unique index, and the fields must be mandatory; optional fields cannot participate in the constraint.

parameters.name: fields

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Optional Prisma-level name for the constraint.

parameters.name: map
parameters.description: Optional database-level mapped name.

parameters.name: where
parameters.description: Optional raw filter expression or field-value object.

@@unique.returns: A model-level compound unique constraint and corresponding unique index.

example.explanation: Ensures an author cannot have two posts with the same title.

useCases.scenario: Prevent duplicate titles within the same author or owner.

useCases.title: Compound business identifier

useCases.title: Database naming
useCases.scenario: Control generated constraint and index names.

interview.question: What does @@unique do?
interview.answer: @@unique defines a compound unique constraint across multiple model fields. Prisma also adds a corresponding unique index for those columns.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to the participating fields? They must all be mandatory, not optional.

interview.question: How do you declare a compound unique constraint?
interview.answer: Use the fields argument with a list such as @@unique([authorId, title]). The combination, rather than either field independently, must be unique.
interview.followUp: How would you make the database object name explicit? Supply the name or map argument in the attribute.

interview.question: How many @@unique blocks can a model have, and when is one required?
interview.answer: A model can contain multiple @@unique blocks. If it has no @id or @@id, a @@unique block is required when it is the model's only unique constraint.
interview.followUp: Can @@unique replace every identifier requirement? No; the model still needs at least one unique identifier, and the documented rule applies when it is the sole one.

keyPoints: It enforces uniqueness on a combination of fields at the model level.
Several different field combinations can each have their own compound constraint.
The declaration also results in a unique index for the selected database columns.
The fields list can include a length modifier for supported fields.
Field entries can specify descending or ascending sort order.
gotchas: Do not include optional fields in the compound constraint.
A model without an ID needs this block when it is the model's sole unique identifier.

@db.summary: `@db` is Prisma’s native database type attribute. It refines a Prisma scalar by selecting the exact provider-specific database type used for the column.
@db.explanation: The `@db` attribute refines a Prisma scalar field with the exact native type used by the configured database provider. Write the provider-specific type after the field declaration; Prisma Migrate then uses that choice when generating the database schema, and introspection adds the attribute when the database type differs from the provider’s default mapping.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Provider-specific native database type, optionally accepting arguments such as a length.

@db.returns: A Prisma schema field annotation that controls the underlying database column type.

example.title: Use native database types
example.explanation: This schema keeps Prisma scalar types while selecting PostgreSQL-specific column types for the email and createdAt fields.

useCases.title: Control string length
useCases.scenario: A string column needs a fixed maximum length rather than the connector’s default text mapping.

useCases.title: Select a specialized database type
useCases.scenario: A field must use a database-specific date, numeric, JSON, or other native representation.

useCases.title: Represent existing column types
useCases.scenario: A schema must reproduce an existing database’s non-default column types after introspection.

interview.question: What does the `@db` attribute do?
interview.answer: `@db` is a native database type attribute. It preserves the Prisma scalar type while selecting a provider-specific database type, such as `@db.VarChar(200)` for a `String` field.
interview.followUp: What determines whether the attribute is valid? The datasource provider determines the available native types and their mapping.

interview.question: Why would a schema use `@db.VarChar(200)` instead of plain `String`?
interview.answer: Prisma scalar types have default mappings in each connector. An explicit `@db` attribute overrides that choice, and Prisma Migrate uses the specified type when creating a migration.
interview.followUp: What happens during introspection? Prisma represents the column with its Prisma scalar type and adds a native attribute when the native type is not the default.

interview.question: How is a native type attribute written?
interview.answer: The attribute is written in PascalCase and is prefixed by `@db`, where `db` matches the datasource block name. Examples include `@db.VarChar(200)` and `@db.Date`.
interview.followUp: Can the same spelling always be reused across databases? No; native types and mappings are connector-specific.

keyPoints: Every Prisma scalar has a connector-defined default database type.
`@db` selects the exact native type that Prisma should create.
Length-constrained strings can use attributes such as `@db.VarChar(200)`.
Migrations honor the native types declared on fields.

@default.summary: @default defines the value Prisma or the database uses when a scalar field is omitted during creation. It accepts literals, supported functions, and database-generated expressions.
@default.explanation: Place @default on a scalar field to supply its value when a create operation omits that field. The value can be a literal, a Prisma-provided function such as now(), cuid(), or uuid(), or a database-generated expression; relation fields themselves cannot receive defaults.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Default expression, such as a literal, function, or database-generated value.

parameters.name: map
parameters.description: Optional mapped database default name; SQL Server only.

@default.returns: A default value for the annotated scalar field.

example.title: Scalar field defaults
example.explanation: This model assigns an automatically generated integer ID, the creation timestamp, and an initial Boolean value when records are created.

useCases.title: Generated primary keys
useCases.scenario: Assign generated identifiers without passing an ID from application code.

useCases.title: Automatic timestamps
useCases.scenario: Set creation timestamps automatically when records are inserted.

useCases.title: Initial field state
useCases.scenario: Initialize flags, counters, JSON values, or scalar lists with consistent defaults.

interview.question: What does @default do?
interview.answer: @default supplies a value when a scalar field is not provided during creation. It may represent a database DEFAULT or use a Prisma ORM-level function, depending on the expression.
interview.followUp: How would you model a default on a relation? Use the scalar field listed in the relation's fields argument; relation fields themselves cannot have defaults.

interview.question: Which kinds of values can @default contain?
interview.answer: Use literals such as false or quoted JSON, and functions such as now(), cuid(), uuid(), and autoincrement() where supported. Prisma-provided cuid() and uuid() are generated by Prisma Client's query engine for all connectors.
interview.followUp: What is required for a JSON object default? Quote the entire JSON value and escape each internal double quote with a backslash.

interview.question: Does Prisma always generate the default value?
interview.answer: For relational databases, a default can become a database DEFAULT value, while some functions are evaluated by Prisma ORM. This distinction affects where the value is generated.
interview.followUp: How are unsupported database defaults represented after introspection? Prisma uses dbgenerated() for defaults that cannot yet be expressed in the schema.

keyPoints: The attribute belongs on scalar model fields and fills in omitted values during record creation.
Some defaults are stored as database-level DEFAULT expressions rather than generated by application code.
Functions such as now(), cuid(), and uuid() can provide generated defaults through Prisma ORM.
Prisma's query engine supplies cuid() and uuid() across connectors.
Scalar-list defaults are available when the database natively supports scalar lists.
gotchas: Do not attach @default directly to a relation field. Put the default on a scalar field that backs the relation instead.
Represent JSON defaults as quoted strings, escaping internal double quotes when defining an object.
A default on a relation's backing scalar can cause the relation to be populated automatically.

@id.summary: @id defines a model's single-field identifier. In relational databases it represents a single-field primary key; compound identifiers use @@id.
@id.explanation: Use @id on one scalar field to make that field the model's single-field identifier and primary key. The field may also use a default generator such as autoincrement(); for MongoDB, the field must additionally map to the underlying _id field.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: Optional field-level arguments and modifiers can be added to the annotated field, such as a default value generator; the referenced page's @id section does not define a standalone parameter list.

@id.returns: Defines the model's single-field ID; it does not return a runtime value.

example.explanation: This model gives each User one integer primary key generated by the database.

useCases.scenario: A model needs one scalar primary key.

useCases.title: Combine with a default generator
useCases.scenario: Records need generated numeric identifiers.

useCases.title: Map MongoDB _id
useCases.scenario: A MongoDB model needs its required document identifier.

interview.question: What does @id do?
interview.answer: @id defines a single-field ID on a model. In relational databases, it represents the model's primary key, while a compound identifier uses @@id instead.
interview.followUp: How would you model an identifier made from two fields? Use a model-level @@id([fieldA, fieldB]) declaration.

interview.question: How many IDs can a Prisma model have?
interview.answer: A model may have only one ID. Put @id on the scalar field that uniquely identifies each record; use @unique for additional independently unique fields.
interview.followUp: Can a model have both @id and @@id? No; the model has one ID, so choose either a single-field or compound definition.

interview.question: How does @id differ across relational databases and MongoDB?
interview.answer: For MongoDB, the identifier must be a single field with @id and @map("_id"). Relational databases can use either a single-field @id or a multi-field @@id.
interview.followUp: What is the relational alternative for a multi-field identifier? Declare @@id with the participating fields at model level.

keyPoints: @id marks one field as the model's single-field identifier.
The ID distinguishes individual records within the model.
Relational databases use @id for a single-field primary key.
Use @@id instead when the identifier combines multiple fields.
gotchas: A model cannot define multiple separate @id fields; use @@id when the identifier is compound.
MongoDB requires the @id field to include @map("_id").

@map.summary: Prisma mapping attributes connect friendly schema and Client names to existing database names. Use @map for fields and enum values, and @@map for models and enums.
@map.explanation: Use @map for a field or enum value, and @@map for a model, enum, or table name. Prisma Client then exposes the schema names while Prisma connects them to the existing database names. Index and constraint defaults use database entity names, even when schema names are mapped.

parameters.name: databaseName
parameters.description: The database name of the mapped field or enum value.

parameters.name: databaseName

useCases.title: Keep a clean Client API
useCases.scenario: An existing table uses plural or snake_case names, but application code should use singular PascalCase models.

useCases.title: Rename fields in the schema only
useCases.scenario: A legacy column name is unclear or inconsistent with current code conventions.

useCases.title: Map enum identifiers
useCases.scenario: Database enum names or values must stay unchanged while schema names improve.

interview.question: What is the difference between @map and @@map?
interview.answer: Use @@map on a model to keep a different table name in the database. Use @map on a field to keep a different column name. These attributes separate Prisma Client naming from database naming.
interview.followUp: How are enum mappings handled? Use @@map for the database enum name and @map for an enum value. In Prisma ORM v7, generated TypeScript uses the mapped enum value.

interview.question: How can you use Prisma names without renaming existing tables?
interview.answer: A model can use a singular PascalCase name such as Comment while @@map("comments") points to the existing comments table. Client code uses prisma.comment, but the database table is unchanged.
interview.followUp: Can a field be mapped too? Yes. For example, content @map("comment_text") makes content the Prisma field and comment_text the database column.

interview.question: How does Prisma name indexes and constraints?
interview.answer: When no explicit names are supplied, Prisma generates names for primary keys, unique constraints, indexes, and foreign keys. The patterns use database table and column names, such as {tablename}_{column_names}_idx for a non-unique index.
interview.followUp: What happens during introspection? Names that follow Prisma's convention may be omitted from the schema, while nonconforming names are added.

keyPoints: Mapping lets the generated Prisma Client use names that differ from the underlying database.
Use @@map on a model when its database table or collection has another name.
Use @map on a field when its database column has another name.
Enum values can use @map, and the enum itself can use @@map.
The default primary-key name follows the table-name pattern with the _pkey suffix.
A default non-unique index name combines the database table name, column names, and _idx.
gotchas: For Prisma ORM v7, mapped enum values are represented by their mapped database values in generated TypeScript, not by the schema names.
Default index and constraint names are based on database table and column names, not only the names written in the Prisma schema.
Long generated index or constraint names can be shortened to fit the database's maximum identifier length.

interview.question: What does @relation do?
interview.answer: @relation adds metadata to a relation field. In a typical one-to-many relation, fields identifies the local scalar foreign key and references identifies the target field it points to.
interview.followUp: How would you model two relations between the same models? Add the name argument to both relation fields and use the same nonempty name on each side.

interview.question: When is @relation required?
interview.answer: The attribute is needed for one-to-one and one-to-many relations on one side together with the corresponding relation scalar. It is also required when relations need disambiguation, for self-relations, and for MongoDB many-to-many relations.
interview.followUp: What must a one-to-one foreign key have? It needs a unique constraint so one related record cannot be linked to multiple records.

interview.question: What do fields and references mean?
interview.answer: A fully annotated relation commonly looks like author User @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]). The scalar authorId stores the foreign-key value, while id is the referenced field on User.
interview.followUp: Which database concepts correspond to this mapping? It corresponds to foreign-key and references constructs in the database.

keyPoints: @relation describes how a relation is represented rather than creating a standalone model field.
For relational databases, the mapping corresponds to foreign-key and references constraints.
Use it for certain one-to-one and one-to-many definitions, ambiguous relations, self-relations, and MongoDB many-to-many relations.
Use relation metadata when you need to customize the underlying relation-table representation.
A custom relation name may be chosen freely, but an empty string is invalid.
gotchas: Put @relation on a field whose type is another model, not directly on the scalar foreign-key field.
Relations between the same pair of models must use a shared, nonempty name on both sides to remove ambiguity.
Define a relation field on each participating model; a lone relation field does not complete the schema relation.

interview.question: What does @unique do, and when must the field be required?
interview.answer: @unique defines a unique constraint for one scalar field, so values in that column must be distinct. It may be optional or required, but it must be required when it is the only unique constraint on a model without an ID.
interview.followUp: How would you enforce uniqueness across several fields? Use the model-level @@unique attribute with the participating scalar fields.

interview.question: Can a model contain multiple @unique fields?
interview.answer: A model can have any number of unique constraints, and @unique can be applied to any scalar field. Each application represents a single-field constraint rather than a compound constraint.
interview.followUp: What is the corresponding syntax for a compound constraint? Use @@unique([fieldA, fieldB]) at model level.

interview.question: What database effect accompanies @unique?
interview.answer: Adding @unique automatically adds a corresponding unique index to the specified column. The database therefore receives both the uniqueness enforcement and its associated index through the schema definition.
interview.followUp: How can the underlying constraint or index name be customized? Supply the optional map argument to @unique.

keyPoints: @unique makes one scalar field uniquely identify values within its model.
The attribute supports both nullable and non-nullable scalar fields.
You may mark multiple fields as unique in the same model.
Use @unique with scalar fields such as String, Int, or DateTime.
Schema application also creates the database's corresponding unique index.
gotchas: If a model has no @id or @@id, its sole @unique identifier cannot be optional.
An optional unique field can still have multiple null values.
Place @unique on scalar fields, not relation fields.

@updatedAt.summary: @updatedAt automatically tracks when a record was last updated. Prisma Client manages the value for DateTime fields when the application does not provide one.
@updatedAt.explanation: @updatedAt is a Prisma schema attribute for DateTime fields. Prisma Client supplies the current time when you omit a value and updates the field when a record changes, while an update with an empty clause leaves it unchanged.

useCases.title: ORM-level timestamp management
useCases.scenario: You want Prisma-managed time values rather than relying on a database timestamp expression.

interview.question: What does @updatedAt do?
interview.answer: It automatically stores when a record was last updated. If the application does not provide a time, Prisma Client sets the field automatically.
interview.followUp: Where is the behavior implemented? It is implemented in the Prisma ORM layer, not as a database-side operation.

interview.question: How is @updatedAt declared?
interview.answer: The field must use the DateTime type, and the attribute is placed after that field declaration. A typical declaration is `updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt`.
interview.followUp: Can it be attached to a String field? No; the documentation specifies compatibility with DateTime fields.

interview.question: What happens during an empty update?
interview.answer: A normal update causes Prisma to refresh the timestamp, but an empty update clause leaves the existing value unchanged. This means no-op updates do not necessarily advance the field.
interview.followUp: How can database-generated timestamps differ from this value? Database functions such as now() run at the database level, while @updatedAt runs in Prisma ORM.

interview.question: What does Prisma Client's `$connect()` do?
interview.answer: `$connect()` explicitly establishes Prisma Client's connection to the data source. Normally, Prisma invokes it implicitly when the first API request or query occurs.
interview.followUp: Why call it explicitly? It can move connection setup to startup so the first user request does not pay the lazy-connection cost.

interview.question: Is `$connect()` required before every query?
interview.answer: It is generally optional because Prisma Client uses lazy connection behavior. The first query opens the connection automatically if the client has not already connected.
interview.followUp: What lifecycle method complements it? `$disconnect()` closes the client and its database connections when they are no longer needed.

interview.question: When is explicit `$connect()` useful?
interview.answer: Call `$connect()` during application startup when the application needs to establish the data-source connection before serving requests. This is useful when the first request must respond immediately.
interview.followUp: How should a short-lived script clean up? Use a `finally` block to call `$disconnect()` after work completes, including when the work fails.

interview.question: What does `$disconnect()` do?
interview.answer: `$disconnect()` closes the database connections established by Prisma Client and stops the process running Prisma ORM's query engine. It returns a promise, so it should be awaited.
interview.followUp: When should it be avoided? In continuously serving applications, avoid calling it after each request because establishing connections again slows request handling and defeats pool reuse.

interview.question: When is explicit disconnection unnecessary?
interview.answer: Most applications do not need explicit connection lifecycle calls. Prisma Client connects automatically on the first query and disconnects when the Node.js process ends.

interview.question: Give a situation where explicit disconnection is appropriate.
interview.answer: Use `$disconnect()` for finite scripts or temporary clients after their work is complete. It is also appropriate when releasing resources explicitly in environments such as Cloudflare Workers.

interview.answer: $executeRaw executes raw SQL intended for operations such as UPDATE or DELETE and resolves to the number of affected rows. It does not return database records.

interview.question: What is the method signature and result type?

interview.followUp: What limitation applies to the SQL text? One call can execute only one query, so multiple semicolon-separated statements are unsupported.

interview.question: What does Prisma Client `$extends` do?
interview.answer: `$extends` creates an extended Prisma Client from an existing client. The extension can contain model, client, result, or query components, and the returned client exposes the added behavior.
interview.followUp: How can several extensions be combined? Chain `$extends` calls or associate multiple extensions with one extended client.

interview.question: How do you add a custom model method?
interview.answer: A model extension adds methods to one or more Prisma models. For example, a method can wrap an existing model operation and be called through the extended model delegate.
interview.followUp: How would you target every model? Use the model extension's `$allModels` structure rather than repeating the method for each model.

interview.question: When should a client-level extension be used?
interview.answer: Client-level extensions add methods directly to the Prisma Client object rather than to a model delegate. They are useful for operations that do not belong to one particular model.
interview.followUp: How can a reusable extension be organized? Define it with `Prisma.defineExtension`, then pass the resulting extension to the client-level `$extends` method.

interview.question: How do you subscribe to Prisma query events?
interview.answer: Configure the desired log level with `emit: "event"` in the Prisma Client constructor, then call `$on()` with the event name and a callback. For query logging, the callback receives query details such as the SQL text, parameters, and duration.
interview.followUp: What happens if the level is configured with `emit: "stdout"` instead? The event callback is not the configured delivery mechanism; use event emission for `$on()` subscriptions.

interview.question: What information is available in a query-event callback?
interview.answer: Use `prisma.$on("query", callback)` after enabling query events in the client configuration. The callback receives an event object that can be used to log `query`, `params`, and `duration`.
interview.followUp: How would you monitor another supported log category? Configure that category with `emit: "event"`, then pass its event name to `$on()`.

interview.question: What is the purpose of `$on()`?
interview.answer: `$on()` is Prisma Client's event-based logging subscription method. It lets application code react to emitted log events instead of relying only on Prisma's default stdout logging.
interview.followUp: Why might an application choose event-based logging? It can route structured event details, such as query duration, into custom monitoring or filtering logic.

interview.answer: `$queryRaw` sends raw SQL and returns the actual database records, unlike `$executeRaw`, which returns the number of affected rows. The result is an array whose objects represent database records.

interview.question: How can `$queryRaw` be used safely with variables?
interview.answer: The preferred form is a tagged template such as `prisma.$queryRaw\`SELECT ... WHERE email = ${email}\``. Interpolated variables are handled as parameters, helping protect against SQL injection.
interview.followUp: What should be avoided when incorporating user input? Avoid concatenating input into SQL; use parameterized queries or tagged templates.

interview.question: When is `$queryRaw` appropriate, and what execution limitation applies?
interview.answer: It is useful when a query needs raw SQL, such as a SELECT that Prisma's query API does not express conveniently. The method is available for relational databases supported by Prisma ORM and MongoDB.
interview.followUp: What execution limitation applies to one call? Each method call can execute only one query, so multiple statements must not be appended.

interview.question: What does `$queryRawUnsafe` do, and when is it useful?
interview.answer: It executes a raw SQL string or template string and returns records, such as rows from a `SELECT` query. Unlike the safer tagged-template API, its SQL text can contain dynamically constructed structure.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid injection when a value is dynamic? Use database-specific placeholders and pass values separately, or use `$queryRaw` with interpolation for supported value expressions.

interview.question: Why might an application choose `$queryRawUnsafe` over `$queryRaw`?
interview.answer: It is useful when SQL identifiers such as table names must be dynamic, because `$queryRaw` cannot interpolate table names. The dynamic identifier must nevertheless be trusted or safely allow-listed.
interview.followUp: Why can’t a normal value placeholder solve this? Database placeholders represent values, not SQL identifiers, so a table name cannot generally be bound as a parameter.

interview.question: How can `$queryRawUnsafe` still be used more safely?
interview.answer: It supports standard parameterized queries using provider-specific placeholders: `?` for MySQL and `$1`, `$2`, and later positions for PostgreSQL. Parameterization is safer than concatenating untrusted values into SQL.
interview.followUp: What is the preferred alternative when the query does not require a dynamic identifier? Use `$queryRaw` with a tagged template, because the documentation describes it as significantly safer when used correctly.

interview.question: What are the two forms of `$transaction`?
interview.answer: The array form accepts Prisma Client promises and runs them sequentially as one atomic transaction. If an operation fails, Prisma rolls back the transaction, and the returned array preserves the query order.
interview.followUp: When should the callback form be preferred? Use it when the transaction needs dependent results, conditional logic, or other application code between Prisma queries.

interview.question: How does an interactive transaction work?
interview.answer: The callback form receives a transaction-scoped Prisma Client, commonly named `tx`. Queries invoked through `tx` belong to the transaction, which commits when the callback completes successfully and rolls back when it throws.
interview.followUp: What happens if code inside the callback uses the outer client instead? That query is not made through the transaction-scoped client and therefore is not encapsulated in the callback transaction.

interview.question: Which options can configure an interactive transaction?
interview.answer: The second argument can configure transaction behavior, including `isolationLevel`, `maxWait`, and `timeout`. Isolation levels control how the database handles concurrent transactions, while the wait and timeout settings limit transaction-resource acquisition and execution time.
interview.followUp: How can serialization conflicts be handled? Retry the transaction when the database reports a transient serialization or write-conflict error.

keyPoints: Use the array form when independent Prisma operations should execute in a defined sequence within one transaction.
Use the callback form when business logic or control flow must run between database operations.

Interactive callbacks receive a transaction-scoped client as their first argument.
Call the provided `tx` client for every Prisma query that belongs to the interactive transaction.
Array-form operations run in the order listed, not according to database-client scheduling.
gotchas: Using `Promise.all()` inside a transaction does not make its queries run concurrently; the transaction connection executes them one at a time.

interview.question: What was Prisma Client `$use`, and what replaces it?
interview.answer: `$use` was the older Prisma Client API for registering middleware around queries. In current Prisma ORM, it is replaced by a middleware array passed when the client is created.
interview.followUp: How would you adapt middleware that used one function before and after a query? Split the behavior into the appropriate before-query and after-query hooks, because the current API has no `next()` wrapper.

interview.question: What does a current Prisma middleware contain?
interview.answer: A middleware is a plain object with a name and one or more hook functions. The client invokes those hooks at defined points around a query.
interview.followUp: How is registration performed? Put the middleware object in the `middleware` array in the client setup options.

interview.question: What should an application do with existing `$use` code?
interview.answer: `$use` is deprecated and was removed from Prisma Client in Prisma ORM 6.14.0. Prisma Client extensions were previously recommended as its replacement, while current Prisma ORM 7 documentation uses the `middleware` client option.
interview.followUp: What should a migration target be for the stable Prisma ORM 7 API? Use a middleware object in the client setup rather than calling `$use`.

Registration happens during client construction through the `middleware` option, rather than by calling `$use` afterward.

aggregate.summary: Prisma Client's `aggregate()` calculates summary values such as averages, sums, minimums, and maximums over numeric model fields. Filtering, ordering, and limiting can be combined with the calculation.
aggregate.explanation: Call `aggregate()` on a model delegate to calculate aggregate values across the records that match the query. Select numeric fields with `_avg`, `_sum`, `_min`, or `_max`; filtering, ordering, and limiting can shape the records included before the calculation.

parameters.description: Maximum number of records included in the query.

interview.question: What does Prisma Client's `aggregate()` method do?
interview.answer: `aggregate()` computes summary values over the records matched by a model query. The result contains the requested aggregate keys, such as `_avg`, `_sum`, `_min`, or `_max`, with the selected fields beneath them.
interview.followUp: How would you restrict the input rows? Add query arguments such as `where`, `orderBy`, and `take` to shape the records included in the aggregation.

interview.question: How do you request an average with `aggregate()`?
interview.answer: Use `_avg`, `_sum`, `_min`, and `_max` to select calculations for numeric model fields. For example, `{ _avg: { age: true } }` returns the average age in the `_avg.age` property.
interview.followUp: What should the type handling account for? A nullable aggregated field may produce either a number or `null`, so callers should handle both cases.

interview.question: Can `aggregate()` be combined with other query constraints?
interview.answer: The query can combine an aggregate selection with filtering, ordering, and a row limit. This lets the calculation operate on a deliberately selected subset rather than every record.
interview.followUp: When is `groupBy()` more appropriate? Use grouping when separate aggregate results are needed for each group instead of one result over the matched rows.

keyPoints: The method belongs to Prisma Client's aggregation features, alongside record counting and distinct-value selection.
An `_avg` selection calculates the average for a chosen numeric field.
Use `where` and `orderBy` alongside aggregate selections when the calculation needs a filtered or ordered input set.
The returned aggregate object exposes the computed value through the selected aggregate key and field.
gotchas: When the selected numeric field is nullable, handle a possible `null` result instead of assuming a number.
Aggregate numeric operations apply to number fields such as `Int` and `Float`; do not select unsupported field types.

interview.question: What is Prisma ORM?
interview.answer: Prisma ORM is a typed data layer for TypeScript. It uses a contract to define models and provides typed queries and migrations for supported databases.
interview.followUp: What replaces schema.prisma in ORM 8? The contract replaces it, and contract emit generates the files needed by the application.

interview.question: How do you query related records?
interview.answer: Use the generated db object to query models. For example, db.orm.public.User.include("posts").all() reads users and related posts in the public PostgreSQL schema.
interview.followUp: How do you make the result type-safe? The result fields are typed from the contract, including fields on related posts.

interview.question: What command follows a contract change?
interview.answer: After changing the contract, run npx prisma contract emit. To plan and apply database changes, use the migration commands described by the current ORM documentation instead of the older Prisma 7 workflow.
interview.followUp: What changed from Prisma ORM 7? ORM 8 changes the contract, generated client, query shape, and migration workflow.

keyPoints: It gives TypeScript applications a typed way to read and write database data.
The contract contains the application's data models.
Query results receive types from the contract, including fields in related records.
Use db.orm to access typed queries for the models.
The include operation lets one query load related records.
Transactions group multiple writes so they succeed or fail as one operation.
Run contract emit after editing the contract to regenerate the ORM files.
gotchas: Prisma ORM 8 is not a final release yet.
ORM 8 does not use the @prisma/client package. Import the generated db object instead.
MongoDB support is early access and does not include every PostgreSQL feature.

interview.question: What does the `contains` filter do?
interview.answer: `contains` is a Prisma Client string filter used inside a field condition in `where`. It matches records whose field value includes the supplied substring.
interview.followUp: How would you make the match case-insensitive? Add `mode: "insensitive"` alongside `contains` in the same field filter.

interview.question: How is `contains` written in a Prisma Client query?
interview.answer: Place `contains` in the string field's filter object, for example `title: { contains: "Prisma" }`. The surrounding query can be a normal Prisma Client operation such as `findMany`.
interview.followUp: How can the filter be combined with another condition? Add another field condition or compose conditions with Prisma's logical operators such as `AND` or `OR`.

interview.question: How do you perform a case-insensitive contains query?
interview.answer: The documented example combines `contains: "Prisma"` with `mode: "insensitive"` to match the substring without regard to case. This is useful when users may enter different capitalization.
interview.followUp: What broader query feature contains this operator? Prisma Client filtering uses the `where` option, which supports multiple field conditions and logical operators.

keyPoints: `contains` is one of Prisma Client's string filter operators, alongside operators such as `startsWith`.
The reference documents a query that filters records by a title containing a substring while ignoring case.
String filters are applied through Prisma Client's `where` query option.
A `contains` condition can participate in compound filtering with Prisma's logical operators.
gotchas: Case-insensitive matching requires the `mode: "insensitive"` option; `contains` alone does not request case-insensitive behavior.

interview.question: How do you count records with Prisma Client?
interview.answer: Call the model delegate's count() method, such as prisma.user.count(), to obtain the number of matching records. Add where to restrict which records are included.
interview.followUp: How would you count only users with at least 100 profile views? Use prisma.user.count({ where: { profileViews: { gte: 100 } } }).

interview.question: How do you count only records matching a condition?
interview.answer: Pass a where object to count() containing the required conditions. Prisma applies those conditions before returning the count.
interview.followUp: How would you count posts for one author? Filter with where: { authorId: theId }.

interview.question: What can Prisma's count operation count?
interview.answer: The method can count all records or non-null values for a selected field. The returned value is the count of records or qualifying field values.
interview.followUp: What happens when no records match? The count is zero.

keyPoints: Use count() for either a model's records or non-null values of a field.
Calling prisma.user.count() without arguments counts every User record.
Supply where conditions to count only records satisfying a filter.
A numeric filter such as gte can restrict the counted records by profile views.
Filtering by a foreign-key field lets you count a particular user's related posts.

interview.question: What does Prisma Client's `create` operation do?
interview.answer: `create` inserts a new database record and returns the created record. The required input is provided through the `data` object, which can contain scalar fields and nested relation writes.
interview.followUp: How can related records be inserted in the same operation? Use a nested `create` inside the parent record’s relation field.

interview.question: How do you create one User record?
interview.answer: Call `prisma.user.create` with a `data` object containing the new user's fields. Prisma returns the inserted user, including generated values such as an ID and database defaults.
interview.followUp: What happens when a field is omitted? The operation can succeed when the schema or database supplies a generated value or default, provided all required input is otherwise present.

interview.question: When would you use nested `create`?
interview.answer: A nested `create` adds a related record or multiple related records while creating the parent. Prisma connects the nested records to the parent without requiring the caller to manually provide the relation's foreign key.
interview.followUp: Why can the foreign key be omitted for nested posts? Prisma derives and fills it from the parent record created by the operation.

keyPoints: The `create` operation inserts a new record into the database.
A record may be created with only the fields required by the generated input type.
Nested creation can write a parent and related records in one operation.
gotchas: Nested creation is available for related records, but it is a distinct use of the same operation inside a parent write.

createMany.explanation: Call `createMany()` on a model delegate with a `data` array containing records to insert. The operation runs in a transaction and returns an object containing the number of records created; `skipDuplicates` can omit rows that violate supported unique constraints.

interview.question: What does `createMany()` return?
interview.answer: `createMany()` accepts a `data` array and inserts multiple records in a transaction. Its result contains a `count` property rather than the created records.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid duplicate inserts? Use `skipDuplicates` where the database supports it, or enforce and handle unique constraints explicitly.

interview.question: Why use `createMany()` instead of repeated `create()` calls?
interview.answer: It is intended for multiple records of the same model in one bulk operation. Prisma documents bulk writes as transactional, so a failed operation rolls back the entire write.
interview.followUp: What limitation applies to relations? A top-level bulk insert cannot perform nested relation creation or connection.

interview.question: When can `skipDuplicates` be used?
interview.answer: `skipDuplicates` tells Prisma to omit records that conflict with supported unique constraints. The option is unavailable for MongoDB, SQL Server, and SQLite.
interview.followUp: Does skipping duplicates guarantee every input row is inserted? No; conflicting rows are omitted, so the returned count can be lower than the input length.

keyPoints: Use it to insert several records of one model as a single transactional bulk operation.
SQLite supports the operation, although it does not support the `skipDuplicates` option.
The result reports the number of records created through its `count` field.
gotchas: Do not use `skipDuplicates` with MongoDB, SQL Server, or SQLite.
A top-level `createMany()` cannot create or connect related records.

interview.question: What does createManyAndReturn() do?
interview.answer: createManyAndReturn() inserts multiple records and returns the resulting objects. It supports select, omit, and include to control the returned data.
interview.followUp: Which databases support it? Prisma documents support for PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, and SQLite.

interview.question: What are the main options?
interview.answer: The data argument contains an array of UserCreateManyInput values. Optional select, omit, include, and skipDuplicates arguments change the result or insert behavior.
interview.followUp: Which field controls duplicate handling? skipDuplicates skips rows that conflict with unique or ID fields when the database supports the needed conflict operation.

interview.question: What limitations should callers handle?
interview.answer: The returned array order is not guaranteed. Also, nested relation writes are not allowed inside a top-level createManyAndReturn() call.
interview.followUp: How can related records be written? Use a supported nested write in create() or update(), or use separate operations suited to the relation.

interview.question: How does Prisma cursor pagination work?
interview.answer: Cursor pagination uses a unique, sequential value to bookmark a position in the result set. The next query supplies that value through cursor, sets take for the page size, and commonly uses skip: 1 to exclude the bookmark record.
interview.followUp: When is offset pagination preferable? Use it when users need to jump directly to a numbered page.

interview.question: What constraints apply to the cursor field?
interview.answer: The cursor should identify a unique, sequential column such as an ID or timestamp. orderBy must sort by that cursor so Prisma can continue from a deterministic position.
interview.followUp: What happens if the cursor value is guessed? Pagination can begin at an unknown location because the guessed value may not correspond to the intended position.

interview.question: How do you paginate backwards?
interview.answer: Set take to a negative value to page backwards. The cursor still marks the known position, while the negative page size requests records in the reverse direction.
interview.followUp: Can cursor pagination jump to page 400? No; the preceding pages must be requested to discover the appropriate cursor.

keyPoints: Use cursor with take to request a bounded result set relative to a known position.
The cursor represents the current position, allowing a subsequent query to continue from there.
Typical cursor fields are IDs or timestamps, provided they satisfy the required ordering properties.
Pass the final record's cursor value into the next query to retrieve the following batch.
gotchas: Set skip: 1 when continuing forward; otherwise the record used as the cursor appears again.
The cursor field must be unique and sequential, and the query must sort by that same field.
Cursor pagination cannot directly navigate to an arbitrary numbered page.

interview.question: What is Prisma ORM?
interview.answer: Prisma ORM is a Node.js and TypeScript ORM. It provides a data model, automated migrations, type safety, and editor auto-completion. Applications use Prisma Client to access database data.
interview.followUp: How does Prisma help when the data model changes? Define the new model shape, create a migration, review it, and apply it to the database.

interview.question: How does Prisma provide type safety?
interview.answer: The schema defines models, fields, and relationships. Prisma uses it to generate a typed client that matches the data model, so many query mistakes can be found while writing TypeScript.
interview.followUp: What happens if the database already exists? Introspect the existing tables and use the result as the starting model.

interview.question: What problem does Prisma Migrate solve?
interview.answer: Prisma Migrate tracks changes to the database structure. After changing the schema, generate a migration, review it, and apply it so the database matches the model.
interview.followUp: Why review a migration before applying it? A migration can change or remove database structures, so reviewing it helps catch unsafe changes.

It includes tools for database migrations, compile-time type checking, and editor completion.
Prisma Client is the generated, type-safe API that application code uses to query the database.

interview.answer: A data source is the datasource block in a Prisma schema. It specifies how Prisma connects to a database, including the provider and connection URL.

interview.question: What is Prisma.Decimal, and what library powers it?
interview.answer: Prisma.Decimal is the Prisma Client representation for schema fields of type Decimal. It is implemented with the Decimal.js library, so Decimal.js operations can be used on values before they are written.
interview.followUp: How would you add one to a Decimal value? Construct it with Prisma.Decimal and call `.plus(1)` before supplying it to the query data.

interview.question: How do you write a Decimal value with Prisma Client?

interview.followUp: Can arithmetic be performed during construction of query data? Yes; the documented pattern is `new Prisma.Decimal(24.454545).plus(1)`.

interview.question: What database limitation applies to Decimal fields?

interview.question: Why must delete() follow where()?
interview.answer: The query must include where() first. PostgreSQL checks this at compile time, while MongoDB checks at runtime and reports ORM.WHERE_MISSING.
interview.followUp: Why is this required? It prevents an accidental unfiltered delete that could remove an unpredictable row or every row.

interview.question: How does PostgreSQL choose the row to delete?
interview.answer: On PostgreSQL, delete() can use query refinements before deletion, so it removes the row that first() would select. If no row matches, it returns null.
interview.followUp: What happens with limit(0)? No row is selected, so delete() removes nothing and returns null.

keyPoints: delete() removes one matching row and returns that row. It returns null when no row matches.

interview.question: How do you delete only selected records?
interview.answer: An empty filter can delete every record for the selected model. A `where` condition narrows the operation to matching records, such as users whose email contains a particular string.
interview.followUp: What risk does an omitted filter create? It can remove the entire model's dataset, so construct and validate the filter deliberately before executing it.

interview.question: How should several bulk deletions be coordinated?
interview.answer: Multiple `deleteMany` operations can be placed in `$transaction([])`. Prisma executes the batch as a transaction, and dependent deletions should be ordered so child records are removed before parent records.
interview.followUp: What happens if one operation fails? The transaction rolls back the entire operation, preserving atomicity.

interview.question: What does Prisma Client's `endsWith` filter do?
interview.answer: `endsWith` is a Prisma Client string filter used inside a field condition in `where`. For example, `{ email: { endsWith: "prisma.io" } }` selects users whose email ends with that text.
interview.followUp: How would you match either of two suffixes? Use `OR` with separate field filters, such as `{ OR: [{ email: { endsWith: "gmail.com" } }, { email: { endsWith: "company.com" } }] }`.

interview.question: Where is `endsWith` placed in a Prisma query?
interview.answer: It is applied as a nested condition on the field being filtered, rather than as a top-level query option. A `findMany` query can therefore use it under `where.email`.
interview.followUp: How can an exclusion be added? Put a matching condition under `NOT`, for example a `NOT` filter for emails ending in an administrative domain.

interview.question: Can `endsWith` be combined with other conditions?
interview.answer: `endsWith` can participate in compound filtering with Prisma's logical operators. This lets a query include records matching alternative suffixes or exclude records matching an unwanted suffix.
interview.followUp: Can the same approach filter JSON values? The reference page also documents JSON-specific operators such as `string_ends_with`, which are distinct from the scalar string filter.

interview.question: What does `findUnique()` query?
interview.answer: `findUnique()` retrieves one record by ID or by a field marked unique. Its `where` filter can also use a compound unique key, and the result may be null if no record matches.
interview.followUp: How would you make absence exceptional? Use `findUniqueOrThrow()`, which retrieves the record in the same way but throws a `PrismaClientKnownRequestError` when none is found.

interview.question: How do you query with a compound unique constraint?
interview.answer: A compound unique constraint is represented in `where` by its generated compound key, whose value is an object containing each constrained field. This lets the query identify one record using the combined unique values.
interview.followUp: Can a compound unique key be used with arbitrary query methods? No; the documentation limits compound ID and compound unique constraint filters to unique queries such as `findUnique()` and `findUniqueOrThrow()`, as well as update, delete, and upsert operations.

interview.question: How can the returned payload be shaped or extended?
interview.answer: Use `select` to choose returned scalar fields and nested relation fields, or `include` to include relations. The result can also be followed with the fluent API to fetch related data when the preceding call returns a single object.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies to fluent chaining? Each preceding call must return only one object, such as a `findUnique()` result or a to-one relation.

keyPoints: A field declared unique can be used to retrieve the matching record.
The method replaced the older `findOne` API in Prisma 2.12.0.
The throwing variant uses the same lookup approach as `findUnique()`.
For a related single record, Prisma Client applies a unique filter to select the appropriate relation.
gotchas: Do not assume a missing record is returned as null when using `findUniqueOrThrow()`; that variant throws a `PrismaClientKnownRequestError` instead.

findUniqueOrThrow.summary: findUniqueOrThrow retrieves one record using a unique lookup and throws PrismaClientKnownRequestError when no record matches. Unlike findUnique, its successful result is non-nullable.
findUniqueOrThrow.explanation: Call this Prisma Client method when a unique lookup must succeed. It performs the same lookup as findUnique, but throws PrismaClientKnownRequestError when no matching record exists, so successful results are non-nullable.

interview.question: How does findUniqueOrThrow behave when no record exists?
interview.answer: It retrieves one record using the same unique lookup rules as findUnique. If no record matches, it throws PrismaClientKnownRequestError instead of returning null.
interview.followUp: What type does it return on success? A non-nullable model type, so callers do not need a null check after a successful await.

interview.question: How does its return type differ from findUnique?
interview.answer: The method's result is non-nullable, unlike findUnique, whose result can be a model or null. This makes absence an exception path rather than a value path.
interview.followUp: When is findUnique preferable? Use it when a missing record is expected and should be represented as null rather than an exception.

interview.question: What transaction limitation does the documentation describe?
interview.answer: It cannot be used safely with sequential operations in the array form of $transaction when rollback is required. A thrown PrismaClientKnownRequestError does not roll back the other array operations.
interview.followUp: What transaction form should be used instead? Use an interactive transaction callback so the operations can be rolled back when the lookup throws.

keyPoints: A missing matching record produces PrismaClientKnownRequestError.
TypeScript can treat the successful result as present without a null check.
The successful result is the model record rather than a nullable model-or-null union.
Interactive transactions are the documented workaround when transactional rollback is needed.
gotchas: In an array-form transaction, a not-found error does not roll back earlier operations; use an interactive transaction when atomic rollback is required.
Handle the thrown error explicitly, especially when the call follows writes in a sequential transaction.

interview.question: What is the purpose of a generator block?
interview.answer: A `generator` block defines which assets Prisma creates when `prisma generate` runs. Its name is an identifier for the block, while `provider` selects the generator implementation.
interview.followUp: How do you control where the generated client is written? Set the required `output` field to a path in the generator block.

interview.followUp: What happens after configuration? Running `prisma generate` reads the schema and generates the customized client in that output directory.

interview.question: Can a Prisma schema define multiple generators?
interview.answer: A schema can contain one or more generators, and each generator determines assets produced by `prisma generate`. The command processes the generators defined in the schema.
interview.followUp: How can a project use more than one generator? Add multiple named generator blocks, each configured for its own provider and supported options.

groupBy.summary: Prisma Client `groupBy()` groups records by one or more fields and calculates aggregates for each group. It supports pre-group filtering with `where`, post-group filtering with `having`, and ordering grouped results.
groupBy.explanation: Call `groupBy()` on a Prisma Client model with one or more fields in `by`. Prisma filters matching records with `where`, forms groups, calculates requested aggregates such as `_count` or `_avg`, and can filter completed groups with `having` or sort them with `orderBy`.

interview.question: What does Prisma Client `groupBy()` do?
interview.answer: `groupBy()` groups records by the fields in `by` and computes requested aggregates for each group. For example, `_sum`, `_avg`, `_min`, `_max`, and `_count` can be used to summarize grouped data.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid aggregating unwanted rows? Use `where`, because it filters records before grouping; use `having` only when filtering completed groups by aggregate values.

interview.question: What is the difference between `where` and `having` in `groupBy()`?
interview.answer: `where` filters individual records before Prisma creates groups. `having` filters whole groups afterward and can compare aggregate values such as an average or sum.
interview.followUp: Why can `having` be more expensive than `where`? It operates after grouping, so the database may need to form groups from more input rows first.

interview.question: How are grouped fields selected and returned?
interview.answer: The fields named in `by` are returned automatically, and Prisma does not allow `select` with `groupBy()`. A single grouping field can use the shorthand string form instead of an array.
interview.followUp: How can you order grouped results? Add `orderBy`, including aggregate ordering such as ordering by a count or average.

keyPoints: Use `by` to create groups from one field or a combination of fields.
Request aggregate calculations independently for every resulting group.
For one grouping field, `by: 'fieldName'` is a supported shorthand.
Prisma provides separate filters for input records and completed groups.
Grouping fields appear in each result without a separate selection clause.
Grouped aggregation is useful for per-category statistics such as averages.
gotchas: `select` is not supported for this operation; fields listed in `by` are returned automatically.
Putting row-level filters in `where` prevents excluded records from contributing to aggregates.
Use `having` for aggregate-based group filtering, not `where`.

gt.summary: Prisma Client lets you compare two fields from the same model in a non-unique filter. Use `<model>.fields.<field>` as the comparison value.
gt.explanation: Use the model's `fields` property to compare one field with another field in the same model. The fields must have matching types. This works with non-unique filters, such as `findMany`; unique filters need raw SQL.

parameters.name: where
parameters.description: The comparison filter, such as `lte`, containing a field reference from the same model.

parameters.name: <model>.fields.<field>
parameters.description: The referenced field on the queried model.

gt.returns: The selected records that satisfy the field-to-field comparison.

interview.question: How do you compare two columns in the same table?
interview.answer: Use `<model>.fields` inside a non-unique filter. For example, `quantity: { lte: prisma.product.fields.warnQuantity }` compares two columns in the same row.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to the compared fields? They must be fields on the same model and have the same type.

interview.question: What type and model restrictions apply?
interview.answer: The fields must have the same type, and both must belong to the model being queried. A cross-model comparison through one model's `fields` property is not valid.
interview.followUp: How can fields from separate models be compared? Use standard relation queries rather than the same-model `fields` comparison.

interview.question: When must you use raw SQL?
interview.answer: The `fields` comparison is for non-unique filters. For `findUnique` or `findUniqueOrThrow`, or when comparing a field with a unique constraint, use a raw query.
interview.followUp: What additional `groupBy` rule applies? Referenced fields used in `having` must also appear in `by`.

keyPoints: Use a model's `fields` property to compare two columns in the same table.
Each model exposes its fields through the model-specific `fields` property.
The two compared fields must have the same data type.
Comparisons involving separate models can use normal relation queries.
gotchas: Both fields in the comparison must use the same type. Comparing a string field with an integer field causes a type error.
The compared fields must belong to the same model. Use standard queries for comparisons involving separate models.
Use raw SQL when the comparison is needed in a unique filter.
When using `groupBy` with `having`, include every referenced field in `by`.

gte.summary: `gte` filters Prisma Client query results to values greater than or equal to a supplied threshold. It is used inside a field condition in a `where` clause.
gte.explanation: Use `gte` inside a Prisma Client field filter to keep records whose value is greater than or equal to the supplied value. It works with orderable scalar values, including numbers and dates, and is typically placed within a model query's `where` object.

parameters.type: A value compatible with the filtered field, such as a number or Date
parameters.description: The comparison value `x`; records are retained when the selected field is greater than or equal to it.

gte.returns: A Prisma Client query result containing records whose selected field value is greater than or equal to the supplied comparison value.

useCases.title: Range filtering

interview.question: What does Prisma Client's `gte` filter do?
interview.answer: `gte` means greater than or equal to. In a `where` filter, it keeps records whose field value meets or exceeds the comparison value.
interview.followUp: How would you express an inclusive date range? Use `gte` for the lower bound and combine it with `lte` for the upper bound.

interview.question: How is `gte` written in a Prisma `where` clause?
interview.answer: Place `gte` under the field being filtered, for example `likes: { gte: 9 }`. The comparison value must be compatible with that field's type.
interview.followUp: What should be used for a strict lower bound? Use `gt`, which excludes records equal to the comparison value.

interview.question: What kinds of values can be compared with `gte`?
interview.answer: The operator can compare orderable values such as numeric fields and dates. A date filter supplies a JavaScript `Date`, allowing the query to select records on or after that timestamp.
interview.followUp: How can the upper boundary also be inclusive? Add `lte` with the desired ending date in the same field filter.

keyPoints: `gte` includes records whose field value equals the threshold as well as records above it.
Use the operator beneath a numeric field in a `where` object to apply an inclusive minimum.
Date fields can use `gte` to select records from a specified point in time onward.

interview.question: What is Prisma Client?
interview.answer: Prisma Client is a generated, type-safe query builder based on the application's Prisma schema. It gives model-specific methods and typed results.
interview.followUp: How does the client know the available models? It gets them from the schema during client generation.

interview.question: How do you read records with Prisma Client?
interview.answer: A basic query creates a PrismaClient instance and calls a model method such as user.findMany(). The result is an array of plain JavaScript objects.
interview.followUp: What could you add to findMany()? Filters, relation selections, ordering, or other query options.

include.summary: `include` adds specified related records to a Prisma Client query result. The related data is returned nested under each parent record, and nested `select` can narrow the relation's fields.
include.explanation: Use `include` in a Prisma Client query to request related records alongside each parent record. The relation fields are returned nested on the parent, and a nested `select` can limit the fields returned from an included relation.

interview.question: What does Prisma Client's `include` option do?
interview.answer: `include` defines which relations Prisma Client includes in the returned result. It is used for nested reads, such as returning a user's posts or profile with the user.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce the included relation's payload? Use a nested `select` inside `include` to choose particular related fields.

interview.question: What is returned by default, and how does `include` change it?
interview.answer: By default, Prisma Client returns all scalar fields for the queried model but no relations. Adding `include` requests specified relations and returns them nested under the parent record.
interview.followUp: What alternative is available when you need a precisely shaped result? Use `select`, which can choose scalar fields and relations explicitly.

interview.question: How can Prisma load included relations?
interview.answer: The relation load strategy can be selected at the top level for queries supporting `include` or `select`. `join` uses a database-level join or correlated subqueries, while `query` sends multiple queries and combines results in the application.
interview.followUp: When might `query` be preferable? It can be useful when reducing database-server resource use or when profiling shows application-level joining performs better.

keyPoints: Set a relation field to `true` inside `include` to return that related data with each parent record.
An included relation can contain a nested `select`, allowing the query to return only selected fields from that related model.
Queries using `include` or `select` can choose a relation loading strategy at the outermost query level.
gotchas: Including a relation does not require returning every field from that relation; use a nested `select` when you need a narrower shape.

interview.question: What does `isNot` do in a Prisma `where` clause?
interview.answer: `isNot` is a Prisma Client relation filter for excluding records whose related record matches nested criteria. For example, `author: { isNot: { name: "Bob" } }` returns posts whose author is not Bob.
interview.followUp: How would you filter a relation-list instead? Use the list-relation filters documented for to-many relations, rather than the to-one `isNot` option.

interview.question: How is the nested value of `isNot` interpreted?
interview.answer: Place `isNot` under a to-one relation field and provide the related record's field conditions as its value. Prisma returns parent records for which the related record does not satisfy those conditions.
interview.followUp: What if the requirement is to exclude several different author conditions? Combine relation filters with Prisma's logical operators such as `NOT`, `AND`, or `OR` as appropriate.

interview.question: Show a practical `isNot` query.
interview.answer: A typical query is `prisma.post.findMany({ where: { author: { isNot: { name: "Bob" } } } })`. It filters posts according to properties of the related author and excludes matching authors.
interview.followUp: Can `isNot` be used with composite types? Yes; Prisma's reference also documents it for composite fields, where it excludes composites that match the supplied object.

The documented relation use is for to-one relations, such as a post's author.

interview.question: How does where() filter records?
interview.answer: where() narrows a collection to matching rows. PostgreSQL accepts a callback with column operators or an object of exact field-value matches.
interview.followUp: How would you combine conditions? Call where() more than once; the filters are combined with AND.

interview.question: What does select() do?
interview.answer: select() limits the returned scalar fields to the names supplied. The result objects contain only those selected fields.
interview.followUp: How would you load related records too? Use include(), optionally refining the related PostgreSQL collection.

interview.question: When should whereUnique() be used?
interview.answer: whereUnique() targets a single row using a primary key or unique constraint. It is PostgreSQL-only, and its input must include every field of one such key.
interview.followUp: What restriction follows from it? Methods that address many rows, such as all() and orderBy(), become compile errors.

interview.question: What does Prisma's `lte` filter do?

interview.question: How is `lte` written in a Prisma Client query?

interview.question: Can `lte` compare one column with another?
